title: Physics — Forces and elasticity
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Physics — Forces and elasticity — combined-science-trilogy-8464-derived, section 4.5.3.
meta_desc: GCSE Combined Science (AQA) practice covering Physics — Forces and elasticity, specification section 4.5.3.
final_note: You worked through Physics — Forces and elasticity — 21 specification statements.

concepts.def: A change in the shape of an object caused by forces acting on it. An object may be deformed by stretching it, by bending it or by compressing (squashing) it.
Making an object longer by pulling its ends apart. Examples include a rubber band pulled between two hands and a spring hanging from a stand with a weight on the end.
Making an object shorter by pushing its ends towards each other. Examples include the suspension spring of a parked car and a spring squashed between a hand and the bench.
Changing the shape of an object so that one side is stretched while the other side is compressed, for example a diving board pushed down at the free end while the fixed end is held.

concepts.term: Why more than one force is needed
concepts.def: To change the shape of a stationary object, more than one force must be applied. A single force would produce a resultant force, and the object would accelerate away instead of changing shape.
Deformation from which an object returns to its original shape and length once the deforming forces are removed.
Deformation after which an object does not return to its original shape and length when the deforming forces are removed; it stays permanently changed.
The increase in length of an object compared with its original, unloaded length. Extension = stretched length - original length.
Two quantities are directly proportional when a graph of one against the other is a straight line through the origin, so doubling one doubles the other.
The point beyond which the extension of an object is no longer directly proportional to the force applied. Up to this point the force-extension graph is a straight line through the origin.
The relationship between the force applied to an elastic object and its extension, written as F = k e. It holds up to the limit of proportionality.
The force applied to the spring, measured in newtons, N. For a spring hanging from a stand with masses on it, this force is the weight of the masses.
A measure of the stiffness of a spring: the force needed per metre of extension, measured in newtons per metre, N/m. A stiffer spring has a larger spring constant.
The extension used in F = k e, measured in metres, m. Lengths measured in centimetres or millimetres must be converted to metres before the equation is used.
The same relationship applies when an elastic object is compressed. In that case e stands for the compression of the object rather than its extension.

concepts.term: Work done and elastic potential energy
concepts.def: A force that stretches or compresses a spring does work, and elastic potential energy is stored in the spring. Provided the spring is not inelastically deformed, the work done and the energy stored are equal.
A linear force-extension relationship gives a straight-line graph, so equal increases in force give equal increases in extension. A non-linear relationship gives a curve.
For a linear region, plotting force on the vertical axis against extension on the horizontal axis gives a straight line whose gradient is the spring constant, k.
The energy stored in a stretched or compressed spring, E_e = 1/2 k e^2, valid up to the limit of proportionality. Energy is in joules, J.
When a stretched or compressed spring is released, the elastic potential energy stored in it is transferred to other stores, for example to the kinetic energy store of an object it pushes.

An investigation of the relationship between force and extension for a spring: hang the spring from a stand, add known weights one at a time, and measure the length after each weight so that the extension can be found.

concepts.term: AT 1 and AT 2 in this practical
concepts.def: AT 1 is the use of apparatus to make length measurements; AT 2 is the safe use of apparatus to measure force. Both are used when a ruler and known weights are used on a loaded spring.

concepts.term: Working scientifically and maths skills here
concepts.def: The practical develops skills such as tabulating results, plotting force against extension, drawing a line of best fit, finding a gradient and identifying anomalous results.

mcqs.q: A rubber band is held by a clamp at one end while a student pulls the other end, and the band stretches. Which statement describes the forces that stretch the band?
options: Two forces act on the band, pulling its two ends in opposite directions.
One pulling force acts on the band, along the line of the band.
Two forces act on the band, both pulling it towards the clamp.
The weight of the band is the only force acting, and it stretches it.
mcqs.explain: Deforming a stationary object needs more than one force, and to stretch it the forces must pull the ends apart.

mcqs.q: A car is parked on level ground and the springs in its suspension are squashed. Which pair of forces compresses one of these springs?
options: The weight of the car is the only force acting on the spring.
The car body pushes down on the spring and the axle pushes up on it.
The car body and the axle both push down on the spring from above it.
The spring squashes under its own weight as it hangs there.
mcqs.explain: Compression needs two forces pushing the ends of the spring towards each other.

mcqs.q: Why must more than one force be applied to a stationary object in order to change its shape?
options: A single force on its own is enough to stretch the object into a new shape.
Forces always occur in pairs, so a second force appears without being applied.
A single force would leave a resultant force, so the object would accelerate.
One force by itself will stretch the object, so no second force is needed.
mcqs.explain: With one force there is a resultant force; the object would move off rather than deform, so a second force is needed.

mcqs.q: Which statement describes elastic deformation?
options: The object keeps part of its extra length after the forces are removed.
The object is made of rubber, so it stretches much further than metal does.
The object breaks into pieces as soon as the stretching force is removed.
The object returns to its original shape once the forces are removed.
mcqs.explain: Elastic deformation is defined by full recovery of the original shape when the forces are removed.

mcqs.q: A steel spring is stretched by a very large force. When the force is removed the spring is longer than it was at the start. Which statement is correct?
options: It has been elastically deformed, because its shape changed while pulled.
It has been inelastically deformed, so it has not returned to its original shape.
It cannot have deformed elastically, since steel is not a stretchy material.
It has been inelastically deformed, so the metal has begun to break apart.
mcqs.explain: Not returning to the original length after the force is removed is exactly inelastic deformation.

mcqs.q: A spring is loaded with weights, staying below its limit of proportionality. Which statement about the force and the extension is correct?
options: The extension is directly proportional to the total length of the spring used.
The force is proportional to the extension whatever the load size.
The extension is directly proportional to the force applied to the spring.
The extension is proportional to the spring constant of that spring.
mcqs.explain: This is the specification statement: extension is directly proportional to force below the limit of proportionality.

mcqs.q: What does the limit of proportionality of a spring tell you?
options: The force at which the spring finally snaps and can carry no more load.
The force beyond which the spring will not return to its original length.
The largest length the spring reaches before it stops stretching.
The largest force for which extension stays proportional to force.
mcqs.explain: Up to this force the graph is a straight line through the origin; beyond it, proportionality is lost.

mcqs.q: A spring has a spring constant of 120 N/m and is stretched by 25 cm, which is below its limit of proportionality. Using force = spring constant × extension, what is the force applied to the spring?
Which statement about the quantities in the equation F = k e is correct?
options: The spring constant, k, is measured in newtons, N, as a force is.
The extension, e, is measured in centimetres, cm, in this equation.
The spring constant, k, is measured in newtons per metre, written N/m.
The extension, e, is the whole length of the stretched spring.
mcqs.explain: F is in newtons, k is in newtons per metre and e is in metres.

mcqs.q: A force of 6.0 N stretches a spring by 12 cm. The limit of proportionality has not been exceeded. What is the spring constant of this spring?
options: 50 N/m

mcqs.q: Spring A has a spring constant of 30 N/m and spring B has a spring constant of 90 N/m. The same force is applied to each spring. Which statement is correct?
options: Spring B extends less, because a larger spring constant means a stiffer spring.
Spring B extends more, because a larger spring constant means more stretch.
Both springs extend by exactly the same amount, because the same force is applied.
Spring B extends three times as far as spring A does under this force.
mcqs.explain: Since e = F / k, a larger spring constant gives a smaller extension for the same force.

mcqs.q: A spring is squashed rather than stretched. Which statement is correct?
options: A different equation is needed, because F = k e only covers stretching.
F = k e still applies, with e as the compression of the spring.
No energy is stored, because energy is only stored by stretching a spring.
The spring constant becomes negative when the spring is compressed.
mcqs.explain: The specification states that the relationship also applies to compression, with e as the compression.

mcqs.q: A spring is stretched by a force and is not inelastically deformed. How does the elastic potential energy stored compare with the work done on the spring?
options: The energy stored is slightly less, because some energy is wasted.
The energy stored is much smaller, because a lot of energy is wasted.
No work is done at all, because the spring stays in one place.
The energy stored is equal to the work done on the spring by the force.
mcqs.explain: The specification states that the work done and the elastic potential energy stored are equal in this case.

mcqs.q: A spring is stretched so far that it is inelastically deformed. Which statement about the work done on the spring is correct?
options: The work done is greater than the elastic potential energy stored in it.
The work done is still exactly equal to the elastic potential energy stored.
The work done equals the energy stored, because they are always the same.
No work is done, because the spring does not spring back again.
mcqs.explain: The equality holds only when the spring is not inelastically deformed; here some work is transferred elsewhere.

mcqs.q: A force-extension graph for a spring is a straight line through the origin up to 8 N, and curves above 8 N. Which statement is correct?
options: The curved readings are anomalies and should be left out of the graph.
The relationship is linear up to 8 N and non-linear above 8 N.
The curved part shows the spring becoming stiffer as the load increases.
The curved part is caused by measurement errors in the larger readings.
mcqs.explain: A straight line through the origin is a linear relationship; the curved region above 8 N is non-linear.

mcqs.q: A spring with a spring constant of 2000 N/m is stretched by 8.0 cm, below its limit of proportionality. Using elastic potential energy = 0.5 × spring constant × (extension)^2, how much energy is stored?
The extension of a spring is doubled, and the spring stays below its limit of proportionality. What happens to the elastic potential energy stored in it?
options: It becomes four times as large, because the extension is squared.
It doubles, because the energy is proportional to the extension.
It stays the same, because the spring constant has not changed.
It doubles too, because the energy just follows the extension.
mcqs.explain: E_e = 1/2 k e^2, so multiplying e by 2 multiplies the stored energy by 4.

mcqs.q: A spring with a spring constant of 800 N/m is compressed by 3.0 cm and then released, pushing a trolley along a smooth bench. Which statement describes the main energy transfer?
options: The compressed spring holds no energy, so nothing moves the trolley.
No energy is transferred, because a compressed spring stores no energy.
The elastic potential energy store of the spring empties to the kinetic store.
The energy stored is transferred to the thermal store of the bench.
mcqs.explain: Releasing the spring transfers the stored elastic potential energy to the kinetic energy store of the trolley.

mcqs.q: In an investigation of force and extension, a student records: 1.0 N, 2.0 cm; 2.0 N, 4.0 cm; 3.0 N, 6.0 cm; 4.0 N, 8.0 cm; 5.0 N, 12.0 cm. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: All five points fit a straight line, so k is 50 N/m for the spring.
The first four points give k = 50 N/m, and the last point is off the line.
The spring constant is 0.42 N/m, taken from the last pair of readings.
The spring became stiffer at 5.0 N, because the extension jumped by 4.0 cm.
mcqs.explain: The first four points give a constant 2.0 cm per newton, so k = 1.0 / 0.020 = 50 N/m, and the 5.0 N point does not fit.

mcqs.q: In required practical activity 6, a spring hangs from a clamp stand and weights are added one at a time. Which method gives the most reliable value for the extension?
options: Take the spring off the stand after each weight and measure it flat on the bench.
Read the ruler from wherever you are sitting, since a scale reading cannot change.
Record the length of the loaded spring itself and use that as the extension.
Measure the loaded length at eye level and subtract the original length.
mcqs.explain: The extension is the loaded length minus the unloaded length, and reading a vertical ruler at eye level avoids parallax error.
